title: Lawn and Garden Equipment Manufacturing
one_liner: A mature machinery niche is being reshaped by battery electrification, emissions rules, soft residential demand and tariff-driven input costs.
overview: The industry sits between consumer durables and light machinery manufacturing: demand follows homeownership, residential construction, disposable income, credit availability, commercial landscaping budgets and nonresidential property formation. The 2021 IBIS baseline described a mature, low-margin industry with $8.6 billion of 2021 revenue, moderate import exposure and revenue concentrated in riding equipment, nonriding equipment, and parts. The April 2025 IBISWorld update points to a softer cycle: revenue is expected to decline at a 2020-2025 CAGR of 0.8% to $9.0 billion in 2025, including a 1.8% decline in 2023, after 2021 stimulus and stay-at-home demand produced a 6.8% revenue jump. The 2025-2026 story is less about lawn ownership disappearing and more about mix shift: battery handhelds, robotic mowers and commercial-grade electric platforms are gaining while gas-powered handheld equipment faces tighter state and local rules. At the same time, steel, aluminum, batteries, motors, electronics and imported components are more exposed to tariffs and currency moves, pressuring manufacturers and retailers to raise prices or sacrifice margin.

key_stats.market_size: 2025: $9.0 billion US industry revenue, per April 2025 IBISWorld report listing via Research and Markets.
key_stats.growth: 2020-2025: -0.8% CAGR; 2023: -1.8% annual revenue decline; 2021: +6.8% stimulus-led annual revenue growth, per April 2025 IBISWorld summary.
key_stats.retail_channel_share: 2025: retail channel accounts for 70.0% of industry revenue, per April 2025 IBISWorld summary.
key_stats.establishments: 2023: 146 employer establishments in NAICS 333112, per Census Business Patterns profile.
key_stats.value_added: 2022: $3.114 billion value added for NAICS 333112 in Federal Reserve G.17 NAICS machinery benchmark table.
key_stats.global_context: 2025: global lawn and garden equipment market was $51.88 billion; North America held 39.66% share, implying roughly $20.6 billion North America demand across broader equipment categories.
key_stats.trade_exposure: 2021 baseline: exports equaled 13.0% of industry revenue and imports equaled 27.3% of domestic demand.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022: approximately $9.4 billion US industry revenue, estimated from the 2025 IBISWorld $9.0 billion revenue disclosure and 2020-2025 CAGR path after the 2021 stimulus spike.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022: negative mid-single-digit revenue growth estimate as the 2021 +6.8% stimulus/home-improvement surge normalized; IBISWorld later reported the 2020-2025 period declined at a 0.8% CAGR.
baseline_2022.value_added: 2022: $3.114 billion NAICS 333112 value added, Federal Reserve G.17 benchmark.
baseline_2022.context: The 2021 baseline had projected 2022 growth from $8.621 billion as demand recovered, but the 2025 update indicates the post-2021 normalization was weaker than that old outlook.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers earn revenue by producing powered lawn and garden equipment and replacement parts, then selling through home centers, mass retailers, hardware retailers, outdoor power equipment dealers, distributors, wholesalers, commercial landscaping channels and export markets. Revenue comes from riding mowers and lawn tractors, push and walk-behind mowers, stand-on mowers, trimmers, blowers, hedge cutters, tillers, shredders, wood chippers, batteries, chargers, attachments, blades, motors and replacement parts. Larger commercial and riding equipment relies more on dealer/distributor networks, while smaller handheld and residential equipment is more exposed to retail sell-through and seasonal inventory cycles.
cost_structure: The cost base is materials-heavy. Steel, aluminum, engines, motors, plastic housings, tires, electronics, batteries, chargers and imported components dominate purchases, while labor, plant overhead, freight, warranty reserves, dealer support, R&D and marketing make up the rest. The 2021 baseline put wages at $730 million, or about 8.5% of 2021 revenue, and EBIT-style profit margin at 4.9%. By 2025-2026, tariff exposure on steel and aluminum, higher material/manufacturing costs cited by Toro, and battery/electronics content are the main margin risks, partly offset by pricing, productivity programs and mix shift toward higher-value commercial and robotic equipment.
current_dynamics: Residential demand is soft but not broken. Higher interest rates and housing affordability have cooled new-home turnover and delayed discretionary equipment purchases, while the installed base of homes with lawns still supports replacement demand. Commercial demand is comparatively steadier where golf, grounds, municipal and landscape contractor budgets hold up. Toro reported fiscal 2025 professional segment sales up 1.9% but residential segment sales down 14.0%, a useful read-through for the split. Husqvarna reported 2025 North America demand remained soft, especially handheld and wheeled products, while robotic mowers had momentum. Battery-powered equipment is shifting from consumer handhelds into walk-behind, stand-on and zero-turn platforms, but commercial adoption still depends on runtime, charging logistics, dealer service and total cost of ownership. Import competition remains meaningful, and 2025 tariff escalation on steel and aluminum raises the cost of both domestic production inputs and imported finished goods with metal content.
whats_growing: Battery-powered handheld tools, robotic mowers, autonomous turf-care systems, commercial electric platforms, replacement batteries and chargers, parts/attachments, dealer service, golf and grounds equipment, municipal fleet electrification, and products positioned for California, Colorado and other emissions-restricted markets. Commercial-grade connected equipment and fleet-management features are also gaining value as contractors try to manage labor, uptime and route efficiency.
whats_shrinking: Gas-powered handheld equipment in regulated states, low-end residential gas products exposed to price-sensitive consumers, discretionary upgrades by homeowners, retail inventory restocking after pandemic-era overordering, and manufacturer margin where tariff costs and material inflation cannot be passed through. Residential riding and walk-behind demand is also under pressure when housing turnover slows and consumers defer big-ticket purchases.
recent_developments: 2024-01: California began requiring most new small off-road engines used in lawn mowers, leaf blowers and similar equipment sold in the state to be zero-emission for model year 2024 and later.
2025-04: IBISWorld's updated industry report, listed by Research and Markets, put US industry revenue at $9.0 billion in 2025 after a 2020-2025 CAGR decline of 0.8%.
2025-06: The US increased Section 232 steel and aluminum tariffs from 25% to 50% effective June 4, 2025, increasing cost pressure on metal-intensive equipment supply chains.
2025-06: Colorado Regulation 29 restrictions began for covered agencies during the June 1-August 31 ozone season, limiting use of gasoline-powered push and handheld lawn and garden equipment.
2025-12: Toro reported fiscal 2025 residential segment net sales down 14.0% to $858.4 million while professional segment sales rose 1.9% to $3.624 billion.
2026-03: Husqvarna's 2025 annual report showed SEK 46.6 billion of 2025 net sales and noted soft North American residential demand but continued momentum in robotic mowers.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is mixed but improving at the margin. Replacement demand, commercial grounds maintenance, golf, municipal electrification and robotic mowing should support revenue, while affordability, cautious consumer spending and retail inventory discipline cap residential upside. Deere's 2026 outlook expects US and Canada small agriculture and turf equipment sales to be flat to up slightly from 2025 levels, helped by a modest turf recovery tied to housing and the broader economy. Manufacturers with strong dealer networks, battery platforms, service parts, commercial mowing exposure and tariff mitigation should outperform. The biggest structural shift is from combustion-engine hardware toward battery, software-enabled and autonomous equipment; the biggest cyclical risk is a consumer pullback combined with input-cost inflation.
themes: Electrification of handheld and mower platforms

title: Leather Good & Luggage Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: A small, fragmented US manufacturing base serves premium, niche and made-in-USA leather goods while mass-market handbags, luggage and accessories remain overwhelmingly imported.
overview: This industry covers establishments that manufacture luggage, handbags, wallets, belts, hats, gloves, neckwear and other leather or nonleather accessories. The 2022 baseline described a long-run decline caused by offshoring, low-cost Asian supply and retailer price pressure, partly offset by niche domestic makers focused on premium leather, small-batch production and made-in-USA positioning. Current 2025-2026 indicators point to the same split: travel and apparel/accessories demand are healthy, but US manufacturing volume remains constrained by import competition, high labor intensity, tariffs, and cautious wholesale inventory buying.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 estimate: about $3.2 billion in US industry revenue, broadly in line with the 2023 IBISWorld-published figure of $3.2 billion.
key_stats.growth: 2025 estimate: roughly flat to slightly negative; IBISWorld reported 2023 revenue down 0.6% and a 2018-2023 CAGR of -1.4%.
key_stats.import_penetration: 2023: imports satisfied 95.2% of domestic demand, up from 93.0% in 2022.
key_stats.hs_4202_imports: 2025: US imports of trunks, suitcases, handbags, wallets and similar containers were $11.25 billion, down 2.4% from $11.53 billion in 2024.
key_stats.retail_demand_indicator: 2025: clothing and clothing accessories retail sectoral output was $330.6 billion, up from $313.6 billion in 2024.
key_stats.travel_demand_indicator: 2025: the US was the world’s largest passenger market at 890.1 million passengers, up 1.6% from 2024; global passenger demand rose 5.3% in 2025.
key_stats.producer_price_indicator: June 2025: BLS/FRED leather and allied product manufacturing PPI was 206.840, index Dec. 1984=100.

baseline_2022.wages: 2022: $759 million in wages, equal to about 25.0% of revenue.
baseline_2022.exports: 2022: $1.617 billion; exports were 53.4% of industry revenue.
baseline_2022.imports: 2022: $18.784 billion; imports satisfied 93.0% of domestic demand.
baseline_2022.outlook_at_baseline: 2022-2027 forecast: revenue CAGR of about 0.4% to $3.1 billion by 2027.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers earn revenue from selling finished handbags, luggage, wallets, belts, caps, gloves, neckwear and other accessories to wholesalers, apparel and accessory retailers, brand owners, direct consumers and export customers. Remaining US producers tend to make money through premium materials, short production runs, customization, repairable goods, faster replenishment, private-label manufacturing and made-in-USA branding rather than mass-market volume pricing.

cost_structure.labor: 2022: wages were about 25.0% of revenue because production is skilled-labor intensive and automation is limited.
cost_structure.profit: 2023: EBIT margin was 4.9%; 2022: EBIT margin was 5.4%.
cost_structure.materials: 2025-2026: leather, textiles, plastics, hardware, zippers, packaging and imported components remain core variable costs; leather price movements and tariff-inclusive landed costs are major margin risks.
cost_structure.purchases_and_outsourcing: 2025-2026: many brand owners rely on contract manufacturing or imported finished goods, so domestic factories compete against lower-cost offshore labor and materials.
cost_structure.freight_and_duties: 2025: the removal of de minimis treatment for China/Hong Kong and then global low-value shipments raised compliance and duty costs for import-heavy accessory supply chains.
cost_structure.capital: 2022: capital intensity was low, with the baseline citing about $0.04 of capital investment for every $1.00 spent on labor.

major_players: Shinola Detroit LLC: premium domestic leather accessories, watch straps and small leather goods with made-in-USA positioning.
Korchmar: US leather bag and business-case manufacturer serving premium and private-label customers.
Duluth Pack: domestic canvas and leather bags, packs and outdoor travel goods.
Frank Clegg Leatherworks: US-made premium leather bags and accessories.
Tapestry Inc. / Coach: major US accessories brand owner; 2025 Coach net sales were $5.60 billion, but manufacturing is largely outsourced rather than concentrated in US factories.
Samsonite Group / TUMI / American Tourister: major luggage and travel-bag brand owner; 2025 global net sales were $3.50 billion, with US demand influencing imports and wholesale orders.
current_dynamics: The industry is supported by resilient travel, higher apparel/accessories retail output and premium handbag demand, but most volume growth accrues to importers and global brands rather than domestic factories. 2025 HS 4202 imports fell only 2.4% despite tariff volatility, showing that foreign supply still dominates the addressable US market. Domestic manufacturers are most competitive where buyers value craftsmanship, small batches, repairability, speed, customization and provenance. The weak spots are price-sensitive luggage and basic accessories, where retailers can shift sourcing among Cambodia, Vietnam, China, India, Italy, France and other suppliers.
whats_growing: Premium and luxury leather handbags, especially brand-led products with pricing power; Coach grew net sales 10% in fiscal 2025.
Non-travel bags and lifestyle accessories; Samsonite reported 2025 non-travel net sales up 3.4% while travel products fell 5.8%.
E-commerce and direct-to-consumer channels; Samsonite’s 2025 e-commerce net sales grew 5.7% constant currency.
Made-in-USA, repairable, small-batch and custom leather goods aimed at higher-income consumers.
Alternative and recycled leather materials; Tapestry expanded its 2025 investment in Gen Phoenix recycled leather fiber materials.
whats_shrinking: Mass-market domestic production of basic handbags, luggage and wallets because imports supplied 95.2% of domestic demand in 2023.
Price-sensitive wholesale luggage orders; Samsonite’s 2025 travel product net sales declined 5.8% and wholesale net sales declined 5.4% constant currency.
China-origin HS 4202 imports; 2025 China shipments were $1.77 billion, down from $2.61 billion in 2024.
Middle-market domestic makers without brand equity, customization or quick-turn capabilities.
Legacy department-store and mall-driven accessory sourcing, as retail demand shifts toward DTC, e-commerce and off-price channels.
recent_developments: 2025-04: IBISWorld-published industry listing reported 2023 revenue of $3.2 billion, 2023 revenue decline of 0.6%, and 2023 import penetration of 95.2%.
2025-05-02: US eliminated duty-free de minimis treatment for China and Hong Kong low-value imports, raising duties and filing requirements for many accessory shipments.
2025-07-30: US announced global suspension of duty-free de minimis treatment effective 2025-08-29 for most low-value commercial shipments.
2025-08: Tapestry reported fiscal 2025 revenue of $7.0 billion, up 5%, with Coach revenue up 10%.
2026-01: IATA reported 2025 global passenger demand up 5.3% and US passenger market volume of 890.1 million, up 1.6%.
2026-03: Samsonite reported 2025 net sales of $3.50 billion, down 2.5%, citing soft consumer sentiment, cautious wholesale orders and US tariff impacts.
outlook: The 2026-2030 outlook is low-growth but not structurally hopeless. Domestic factories are unlikely to win back commodity handbag or luggage volume because landed imports remain scale advantaged even after tariffs. The more attractive lane is premium manufacturing: leather goods with visible craftsmanship, short replenishment cycles, customization, repair, traceable materials and wholesale/DTC flexibility. Tariff and de minimis changes may push some brands to diversify sourcing and hold more domestic backup capacity, but high US labor costs mean reshoring is selective rather than broad. Expect modest revenue growth where travel, luxury handbags and made-in-USA positioning overlap, offset by pressure on basic luggage, private-label imports and cautious retailer inventory management.

title: Leather Tanning & Finishing in the US
one_liner: A small, trade-exposed US manufacturing industry that turns hides and skins into leather for automotive interiors, footwear, luggage, apparel and furniture.
overview: Operators tan, curry, dye and finish animal hides and skins, or arrange contract processing, to produce finished leather and dressed furs. The industry is structurally mature to declining because many downstream footwear, apparel and leather-goods manufacturers have moved overseas, taking leather sourcing with them. In 2025-2026, the market is still anchored by chrome tanning and finishing, with demand tied to auto interiors, luxury goods, footwear, luggage and furniture. Public 2025-2026 indicators point to mixed conditions: US new-vehicle sales improved in 2025, cattle and calf supply remained tight in 2026, hide exports recovered in 2025 from 2024 lows, and regulators continued to focus on wastewater and air-toxics controls rather than broad deregulation.

key_stats.market_size: 2025: about $1.2 billion US industry revenue, based on the July 2025 IBISWorld update stating 2023 revenue was $1.2 billion after a 1.9% 2023 decline and the 2022 baseline projection of near-flat revenue through 2027.
key_stats.growth: 2023: revenue down 1.9%; 2018-2023 revenue CAGR down 5.4%; 2022-2027 baseline projected revenue CAGR down 0.1%.
key_stats.profit_margin: 2023: profit margin expected at 3.7%; 2022: profit margin was 3.6%.
key_stats.exports: 2025: US exports of raw hides, skins and leather were $1.18 billion; 2024 USDA hides and skins exports were $859.58 million with China at $433.03 million.
key_stats.auto_demand: 2025: US new-vehicle sales reached 16.3 million units, up 1.8% from 2024; Cox forecast 2026 sales at 15.8 million, down 2.4%.
key_stats.upstream_supply: 2026: US cattle and calves inventory was 94.2 million head on July 1, 2026; 2026 calf crop was estimated at 32.5 million head, down 2% from 2025.

baseline_2022.growth: 2022: revenue up 3.4%; 2017-2022 revenue CAGR down 7.1%; 2022-2027 projected revenue CAGR down 0.1%.

how_it_makes_money: Companies buy or obtain raw hides and skins from slaughterhouses and meat processors, then generate revenue by tanning, retanning, dyeing, finishing and contract-processing leather for downstream manufacturers. Main customers include 2022-2026 automotive interior suppliers, footwear producers, leather goods and luggage manufacturers, apparel makers, furniture manufacturers and exporters serving China, Vietnam, Italy and other leather-product hubs.
cost_structure: The 2022 baseline shows a low-margin cost base with 2022 profit at 3.6% of revenue and 2022 wages at $149 million, or about 12.6% of 2022 revenue. The largest operating costs are 2022-2026 raw hides and skins, wet-blue inputs, dyes, pigments, chromium and other tanning chemicals, wastewater treatment, energy, labor, freight and compliance. Costs are volatile because hide values move with cattle slaughter, export demand and global leather prices, while EPA wastewater rules cover 2026-regulated pollutants including chromium, sulfide, biochemical oxygen demand, oil and grease, suspended solids and pH.
current_dynamics: In 2025-2026, conditions are better than the pandemic trough but still fragile. Automotive upholstery demand improved with 2025 US new-vehicle sales at 16.3 million units, yet Cox projected a 2026 pullback to 15.8 million as affordability and policy effects cool the market. Export indicators improved in 2025, with raw hides, skins and leather exports at $1.18 billion, but China remained lower than its historical role, with 2025 exports to China at $333.37 million versus 2024 USDA hides and skins exports to China of $433.03 million. Upstream cattle supply is tight, with 2026 beef cows down 1% and 2026 calf crop down 2%, supporting hide-price volatility. Sustainability and traceability are increasingly commercial requirements even after July 2026 EU changes removed cattle hides, skins and leather from the EUDR product scope.
whats_growing: 2025-2026 growth is concentrated in automotive leather tied to higher 2025 vehicle builds, premium and heritage leather, vegetable-tanned and lower-impact specialty products, audit-ready traceability programs, and export channels that can use US hides and wet blues. Leather Working Group traceability work in 2025 and 2026 supports demand for slaughterhouse-level or group-level sourcing documentation, especially from brands managing deforestation and compliance risk.
whats_shrinking: Mass-market leather for US footwear, apparel and luggage production continues to shrink as downstream manufacturing remains offshore in 2025-2026. Chrome-tanned commodity leather faces pressure from synthetics, coated textiles, vegan materials and lower-cost foreign tanneries. Domestic employment and enterprise counts remain structurally constrained after the 2022 baseline showed 4,326 employees and a long-term employment CAGR down 4.06% from 2003 to 2022.
recent_developments: 2025-01-31: USDA NASS reported 86.7 million US cattle and calves as of Jan. 1, 2025, down 1% from 2024.
2025-07: IBISWorld's updated report, distributed by Research and Markets, estimated 2023 industry revenue at $1.2 billion after a 1.9% 2023 decline and a 2018-2023 CAGR of -5.4%.
2025-12-17: Cox Automotive estimated 2025 US new-vehicle sales at 16.3 million, up 1.8% from 2024, and forecast 2026 at 15.8 million, down 2.4%.

2026-06-22: EPA finalized minor leather finishing air-toxics amendments and stated source-category risks were acceptable with no identified technology developments requiring further emissions reductions.
2026-07-13: The European Commission updated EUDR scope and removed cattle hides, skins and leather from the covered product list ahead of end-2026 implementation.
2026-07-24: USDA NASS reported 94.2 million US cattle and calves as of July 1, 2026, with the 2026 calf crop down 2% from 2025.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is flat to slightly negative. Revenue should stay near the 2025 $1.2 billion level if automotive and export demand hold, but the 2026 auto-sales forecast decline, tight cattle supply, persistent foreign competition and synthetic substitution limit upside. Higher-value niches such as traceable, specialty, vegetable-tanned and automotive-grade leather can outperform, while commodity tanning remains exposed to price swings, compliance costs and overseas capacity. The 2022 baseline projection of a 2022-2027 revenue CAGR down 0.1% remains a reasonable directional frame, with 2025 export improvement offset by 2026 demand and input-cost risks.
themes: Export exposure to China and Asia
Environmental compliance and chromium wastewater controls
Tight cattle supply and hide-price volatility

title: Libraries & Archives
one_liner: Government-funded public libraries dominate a low-growth, mission-driven industry that is shifting spending toward digital collections, community space, workforce support and archival digitization.
overview: The U.S. Libraries & Archives industry is primarily a public and nonprofit service market, not a conventional for-profit retail market. The IBIS baseline reported 2021 revenue of $18.6B and projected modest growth to $19.6B by 2026, while narrower Census employer-firm receipts captured only $2.38B in 2022 and commercial industry research estimated $3.1B of 2025 industry sales. Public systems still account for the bulk of physical locations and community demand: BLS reported more than 7,500 libraries and archives in 2024-Q3, including 4,996 local-government locations, 2,398 private locations, 224 state-government locations and 136 federal locations. Demand is increasingly hybrid, with physical visits recovering while e-books, e-audiobooks, digital literacy, meeting rooms and archive digitization absorb a rising share of operating attention.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 funding-inclusive industry revenue estimated at $19.3B using the IBIS 2021 baseline and 2021–2027 projected CAGR; 2025 narrow employer/commercial industry sales estimated at $3.1B by Kentley Insights via Research and Markets.
key_stats.growth: 2025 funding-inclusive revenue growth estimated near 1.0%; 2020–2025 narrow employer/commercial sales CAGR reported at 5.1%.
key_stats.locations: 2024-Q3 BLS counted more than 7,500 U.S. libraries and archives, including 4,996 local-government, 2,398 private, 224 state-government and 136 federal locations.
key_stats.federal_support: FY2025 IMLS apportionment provided $294.8M of discretionary budget authority, including $180.0M for LSTA Grants to States and $2.0M for Native American library formula grants.
key_stats.employment_indicator: BLS projected 2023–2033 employment for librarians and library media specialists to rise 3.0% overall, from 142,200 to 146,400.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 funding-inclusive industry revenue estimated at $18.8B, derived from the IBIS 2021 revenue baseline of $18.6B and 2021–2027 projected CAGR of 1.03%.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022 funding-inclusive revenue growth estimated at 1.0% from the IBIS 2021–2027 projection.
baseline_2022.narrow_employer_revenue: 2022 Census/FRED employer-firm revenue for Libraries and Archives was $2.38B.
baseline_2022.context: The 2022 baseline remains larger than Census employer-firm receipts because IBIS-style revenue includes public funding, grants, donations and nonprofit operating support.

how_it_makes_money: Public libraries and archives primarily make money through 2025 local and state appropriations, property-tax-supported library districts, federal and state grants, private donations, endowment income, foundation support, fines and fees that have been declining in many systems, paid research or reproduction services, memberships at private libraries, facility rentals, and contracted archival or records services. Federal grant flow matters at the margin rather than as the main revenue source: FY2025 IMLS budget authority was $294.8M against a funding-inclusive industry base near $19.3B.

cost_structure.labor: 2021 IBIS baseline wages were $6.1B, roughly one-third of 2021 revenue; staffing remains the largest controllable cost because public libraries need professional librarians, archivists, aides, IT staff and branch operations teams.
cost_structure.collections_and_content: 2023 PLA data showed 95.0% of public libraries offered e-books and/or e-audiobooks, and 85.7% cited subscription costs or payment terms as the top constraint on digital content access.
cost_structure.occupancy_and_facilities: 2024–2025 facilities costs are pressured by longer hours, meeting-room demand, security, utilities, deferred maintenance and new branch construction in larger urban systems.
cost_structure.technology: 2023 PLA data showed 46.9% of public libraries offered hotspots for checkout and 95.3% offered some form of digital literacy training, raising spending on broadband, devices, cybersecurity, platforms and staff training.
cost_structure.surplus_profit: 2021 IBIS baseline profit/surplus margin was 3.9%, but most public and nonprofit operators reinvest surpluses rather than distribute profits.

major_players: Library of Congress: FY2025 enacted funding was $852.1M, with FY2026 proposals ranging from $767.6M in the House-reported bill to $852.2M in the Senate-reported bill.
National Archives and Records Administration: FY2025 presidential budget request was $481.1M for preservation, access and born-digital records management.
New York Public Library: a major nonprofit public-library system with FY2025 annual report and financial statements published in 2026.
Boston Public Library: large municipal system with national brand strength in research, civic programming and digital collections.
Los Angeles Public Library: large urban public-library system serving a broad branch network and digital access mission.
OCLC: FY2025 library services revenue was $262.7M, up 10.1% from FY2024, supplying cataloging, discovery and library technology services.
current_dynamics: The industry is stable but politically exposed. Local funding and property-tax bases anchor most revenue, while federal support became a 2025–2026 risk after executive-branch attempts to dismantle IMLS and eliminate IMLS and IAL funding. At the same time, patron behavior is improving: 2025 Urban Libraries Council data for 2024 showed visits up nearly 10%, meeting-space use up 25%, digital-resource demand up 15%, and budgets up 5%, although budgets needed another 5.4% to keep pace with inflation. Cost pressure is concentrated in labor, digital licensing, insurance, facilities and technology modernization.
whats_growing: 2024 digital resource demand grew 15% among Urban Libraries Council respondents, and 2019–2024 digital use rose 58%.
2024 meeting-space use grew 25% among Urban Libraries Council respondents, reinforcing libraries as civic and work-support spaces.
2023 PLA data showed 46.9% of libraries offered hotspots for checkout, up 14.4 percentage points from 2020.
2023 PLA data showed 95.3% of public libraries offered formal or informal digital literacy training.
2025–2026 demand for born-digital archives, metadata, preservation technology and AI-assisted cataloging is rising as federal, local and cultural records shift online.
whats_shrinking: 2024 inflation-adjusted budgets remained tight, with Urban Libraries Council reporting 2024 budgets rose 5.0% but needed 5.4% more to keep pace with inflation.
2025–2026 federal discretionary funding visibility weakened after proposals to eliminate IMLS and IAL, increasing planning risk for grant-funded programs.
2021–2026 print-first circulation and reference models continue losing share to e-books, e-audiobooks, databases, streaming media and remote services.
2025 late-fee revenue remains structurally pressured as more public systems reduce or eliminate fines to improve access.
2025 small and rural libraries face shrinking relative technology capacity because staff time, broadband funding and digital-content buying power lag larger systems.
recent_developments: 2025-03-14: Executive order began an effort to reduce or eliminate IMLS functions, creating federal grant uncertainty for libraries and museums.
2025-05-30: OMB apportionment showed FY2025 IMLS discretionary budget authority of $294.8M, including $180.0M for LSTA Grants to States.
2025-04-11: BLS reported 2024-Q3 counts of more than 7,500 U.S. libraries and archives, led by 4,996 local-government locations.
2026-04-03: White House FY2026 budget proposal requested elimination of IMLS and the Department of Education's Innovative Approaches to Literacy program.
2026-06-05: House Labor-HHS-Education appropriations subcommittee approved level FY2026 funding for IMLS, according to ALA advocacy updates.
2026-04: ALA reported a binding settlement to keep IMLS intact and protect against future dismantling attempts.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is for slow nominal growth and uneven real growth. The IBIS baseline points to about $19.6B in 2026 funding-inclusive revenue, but the more commercial Census/Kentley slice is smaller and more volatile, with 2025 sales of $3.1B and 2020–2025 CAGR of 5.1%. Local funding should keep the industry from sharp contraction, while digital-content licensing, technology upgrades, cybersecurity, staff recruitment and facilities costs limit margin flexibility. The biggest downside risk in 2026 is federal funding instability; the biggest upside is sustained recovery in visits, programs, meeting-room use and digital services that strengthens local budget arguments.

title: Licensed Sports Apparel Stores
one_liner: Physical licensed sports apparel stores sell officially approved team, league, player and college fan gear, with demand tied to live sports cycles, team performance and fan culture.
overview: This industry covers brick-and-mortar retailers that sell officially licensed sports apparel and accessories bearing team, league, player, event or college marks; it excludes online-only sales and licensed products sold primarily through mass merchants and department stores. The 2025-2026 market is healthier than the 2020 pandemic trough because venue attendance, baseball momentum, hockey attendance, women’s basketball and event retail have improved, but the store channel remains structurally constrained by e-commerce, mall traffic weakness, counterfeit alternatives and high wholesale/licensing costs.

key_stats.market_size: $6.9 billion in 2025 estimated U.S. licensed sports apparel store revenue, anchored to the IBISWorld 2020 forecast for store-only sales and updated against 2025 sports-specialty retail recovery indicators
key_stats.growth: +1.9% average 2025 year-over-year growth proxy for U.S. sporting goods, hobby, musical instrument and book store sales; +8.9% average January-April 2026 year-over-year proxy for the same Census/FRED category
key_stats.broader_us_licensed_sports_merchandise_m: $17.3246 billion in 2025 and $18.1675 billion estimated in 2026 according to Grand View Research Horizon
key_stats.licensed_apparel_share: 48.64% of global licensed sports merchandise sales in 2025 according to Fortune Business Insights
key_stats.store_base: 18,104 U.S. establishments projected for 2025 in the baseline store-only industry; Lids reported more than 2,000 physical retail locations across North America, Europe and Australia in 2026 through Fanatics
key_stats.profit_margin: about 5.0% EBIT margin projected for 2025 in the baseline industry, recovering from 2.7% in 2020

baseline_2022.market_size: $6.8 billion in 2022 estimated U.S. store-only revenue, derived from the baseline 2020-2025 IBISWorld trajectory and broader 2022 retail sales normalization
baseline_2022.growth: +0.6% average 2022 year-over-year proxy for U.S. sporting goods, hobby, musical instrument and book store sales from Census/FRED
baseline_2022.context: 2022 was a post-pandemic normalization year: store traffic had reopened, but inflation, inventory normalization and online substitution limited store-channel growth.

how_it_makes_money: Stores earn revenue from retail markups on officially licensed jerseys, caps, T-shirts, hoodies, outerwear, kids apparel, player-name products, championship/event merchandise, college apparel and accessories. High-margin moments include playoffs, rivalry games, championship wins, draft picks, player trades, throwback drops, stadium/event pop-ups and in-store customization such as embroidery or heat-press personalization.
cost_structure: The largest cost is merchandise purchases and licensed wholesale inventory, followed by rent and occupancy for malls, stadiums, airports and campus stores, wages for store staff, shrink and markdowns, payment processing, local marketing and systems. Royalty and licensing economics are typically embedded in wholesale prices, keeping official gear expensive and limiting discount flexibility; profit is sensitive to stale inventory after losing seasons, player movement and missed playoff runs.
current_dynamics: Demand is being pulled in two directions. Physical stores benefit from live-event attendance, impulse buying at stadiums, local team performance, in-person customization and the renewed strength of MLB, NHL and women’s basketball fandom. At the same time, Fanatics-operated league sites, brand sites, marketplace sellers and big-box retailers capture a large share of planned purchases, forcing stores to become more event-driven, localized and experience-led. Consolidation around Fanatics and Lids gives leading operators better access to league data, rapid replenishment and omnichannel rights, while independents face tighter buying power and less exclusive product access.
whats_growing: Women’s sports merchandise, especially WNBA player and team gear, is growing fastest from a small base, with Fanatics reporting 2025 first-half WNBA merchandise sales up more than 500% year over year and player-specific merchandise up 1,000%. MLB apparel is benefiting from 71.409 million 2025 attendance, faster game times and younger audience growth. Soccer event merchandise is expanding ahead of FIFA World Cup 2026, with Fanatics selected in 2025 to operate official on-site retail across 104 matches and fan festivals in 16 host cities. In-store customization, limited drops, retro product, local-market assortments and premium lifestyle collaborations are also growing.
whats_shrinking: Undifferentiated mall stores, generic team basics, slow-moving player jerseys, lower-margin clearance apparel and stores without customization or event adjacency are shrinking. Online channels held a 40.15% licensed sports merchandise distribution share in 2025 according to Fortune Business Insights, making routine replenishment purchases harder for physical stores. Independent operators are also losing leverage as league, team and manufacturer rights concentrate with larger omnichannel platforms.
recent_developments: Dec 2024: Nike and the NFL extended their uniform and sideline apparel partnership through 2038.
Apr 2025: The NHL set a 2024-25 regular-season attendance record at 23.014 million fans, 96.9% of capacity.
Jul 2025: Fanatics reported WNBA merchandise sales up more than 500% year over year for the first half of the 2025 season.
Sep 2025: MLB reported 71.409 million 2025 attendance, its third straight year of attendance growth.
Oct 2025: ESPN reported its most-watched WNBA full season on ESPN networks in 2025, averaging 1.2 million viewers across 49 telecasts.
Dec 2025: Fanatics was selected as official on-site retail licensee for FIFA World Cup 2026 across 104 matches and fan festival events.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is modestly positive for the physical store channel, helped by stronger 2026 retail-sales proxies, FIFA World Cup 2026 event retail, continued women’s basketball momentum and high live-event attendance. Store-count growth should remain limited because e-commerce and big-box competition absorb much of the broader licensed merchandise expansion, but the best operators can grow sales per square foot through stadium shops, campus partnerships, personalization, exclusive drops and faster reaction to player/team news. Expect market growth to trail the broader U.S. licensed sports merchandise market CAGR of 6.1% projected for 2026-2033 because the fastest channel growth is online.
